title: Level 2 project: a wave defence battle system
lesson:
Time to put Level 2 together into one system you could drop into a Unity tower-defence or strategy game: units that fight, squads that hold them, a wave spawner that reacts to deaths, and your own checks that prove the rules hold.

**Part 1: units and squads** (`Battle.cs`)
- `interface IDamageable` (given): `Health`, `IsDead`, `TakeDamage(int)`.
- `abstract class Unit : IDamageable`: `Name`, `MaxHealth`, `Health` (private set), `IsDead` (Health is 0), abstract `Attack`, virtual `Armor` (0), and two events: `EventHandler<int> Damaged` (the health really lost) and `EventHandler Died`. `TakeDamage` subtracts `amount - Armor` (never below 0, never more than the health left) and raises the events. Bad names and health throw.
- `Soldier` (50 HP, attack 8, armor 2), `Archer` (30, 12, 0) and a `sealed Knight` (80, 10, 5).
- `class Squad<T> where T : Unit`: `Add`, `Count`, `Alive`, `TotalAttack`, `Strongest`, `Report()`, built with LINQ.

**Part 2: the wave spawner** (`Spawner.cs`). It plans each wave with a pure method `PlanWave(n)` (n + 1 enemies, and every third wave the last is a Captain), spawns the squad, **subscribes to each enemy's Died event**, and raises `WaveCleared` when the last one falls. This is the event pattern from unit 6 doing real work: the enemies don't know the spawner exists.

**Part 3: prove it** (`SpawnerChecks.cs`). Write checks for `PlanWave` that pass on the real one and catch broken versions, like you did for armor.

How to work, the professional way:
1. Read each part's prompt fully and list the rules as a checklist.
2. Build in small steps: the base class first, then one unit type, test it, then the next. Archie's visible tests are your guide; the hidden ones check the edges.
3. Keep each class to one job. `Unit` knows nothing about waves; `WaveSpawner` knows nothing about how damage is worked out.
4. When a test fails, read the message, then write the smallest code that fixes it.

Why this design matters in Unity: `Unit` becomes a MonoBehaviour on an enemy prefab, `Squad<T>` becomes the list a manager keeps, the events wire to the health bar and the score text, and `PlanWave` stays a plain C# method you can test without even opening the editor. Logic that's separate from the engine is logic you can test, reuse and trust.

After this: Level 3 (files, JSON save games, async, and bigger architecture), or straight into Unity with these classes in hand.

notes: Unit is abstract with an abstract Attack: every kind of unit must say how hard it hits.
Died is raised once, at the moment health reaches 0.
Main subscribes to every unit's Died event; the units never know who is listening.
The sender tells the handler which unit died.
LINQ sums the attack of the units still standing.

exercises.title: Units and squads
exercises.prompt:
Build Part 1 (the interface IDamageable is given):
- abstract class Unit : IDamageable. Protected constructor Unit(string name, int maxHealth): blank name throws ArgumentException, maxHealth <= 0 throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException. Properties Name, MaxHealth, Health (starts full, private set), IsDead (Health == 0), abstract int Attack, virtual int Armor (0).
  Events: `public event EventHandler<int> Damaged;` and `public event EventHandler Died;`.
  TakeDamage(amount): negative throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException; a dead unit ignores it. Health lost = amount - Armor, at least 0 and at most the Health left. If it is more than 0, lower Health, raise Damaged with the health lost, and if now dead raise Died (once).
  ToString(): "Amina 50/50".
- Soldier(name): 50 HP, Attack 8, Armor 2. Archer(name): 30 HP, Attack 12, Armor 0. sealed Knight(name): 80 HP, Attack 10, Armor 5.
- class Squad<T> where T : Unit: Add(T unit) (null throws ArgumentNullException), Count (all members), List<T> Alive, int TotalAttack (alive only), T Strongest (alive with the most Health, ties by name A to Z, null if none), string Report() (alive units A to Z by name, joined with ", ", or "(all down)").

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var s = new Soldier("Amina"); var a = new Archer("Juma"); var k = new Knight("Otieno"); return s + " " + s.Attack + " | " + a + " " + a.Armor + " | " + k + " " + k.Armor; }))()
tests.name: three kinds of unit

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var k = new Knight("K"); var log = new List<int>(); k.Damaged += (s, d) => log.Add(d); k.TakeDamage(12); k.TakeDamage(3); return k.Health + " [" + string.Join(",", log) + "]"; }))()
tests.name: armor and the Damaged event

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var a = new Archer("A"); int deaths = 0; a.Died += (s, e) => deaths++; a.TakeDamage(25); a.TakeDamage(25); a.TakeDamage(25); return a.Health + " " + a.IsDead + " " + deaths; }))()
tests.name: dies once

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var sq = new Squad<Unit>(); sq.Add(new Soldier("Zed")); sq.Add(new Archer("Ali")); sq.Add(new Knight("Kim")); return sq.TotalAttack + " " + sq.Strongest.Name + " | " + sq.Report(); }))()
tests.name: a mixed squad

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var sq = new Squad<Archer>(); var a = new Archer("A"); sq.Add(a); a.TakeDamage(100); return sq.Report() + " " + sq.TotalAttack + " " + (sq.Strongest == null) + " " + sq.Count; }))()
tests.name: everyone down

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var a = new Archer("A"); var log = new List<int>(); a.Damaged += (s, d) => log.Add(d); a.TakeDamage(20); a.TakeDamage(20); return string.Join(",", log); }))()
tests.name: can't lose more health than is left

tests.call: typeof(Knight).IsSealed + " " + typeof(IDamageable).IsAssignableFrom(typeof(Unit)) + " " + typeof(Unit).IsAbstract
tests.name: the design

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { new Soldier("S").TakeDamage(-1); return "no error"; }))()
tests.name: negative damage

tests.call: new Archer(" ")
tests.name: blank name

hints: Start with Unit and Soldier only, and get the first test passing. Then Archer and Knight are three lines each.
TakeDamage: int taken = Math.Min(Health, Math.Max(0, amount - Armor)); if (taken == 0) return; Health -= taken; Damaged?.Invoke(this, taken); if (IsDead) Died?.Invoke(this, EventArgs.Empty);
Squad: keep a private List<T>; Alive => members.Where(u => !u.IsDead).ToList(); Strongest => Alive.OrderByDescending(u => u.Health).ThenBy(u => u.Name).FirstOrDefault();

exercises.title: The wave spawner
exercises.prompt:
Part 1 is included, finished. Write class WaveSpawner:
- static List<string> PlanWave(int wave): wave < 1 throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException. Otherwise wave + 1 names "Grunt 1", "Grunt 2"...; on waves 3, 6, 9... the LAST name is "Captain" instead.
- Squad<Unit> SpawnNext(): if the current wave still has living enemies, throw InvalidOperationException. Otherwise add 1 to Wave, make a Soldier for each Grunt name and a Knight for "Captain", subscribe to each one's Died event, store the squad in Enemies, raise WaveStarted(this, Wave) and return the squad.
- When an enemy dies, add 1 to Kills; when the last one of the wave dies, raise WaveCleared(this, Wave).
- string Summary(): "No wave yet" before the first wave, else "Wave 2: 1/3 alive, 34 HP left" (alive count / squad size, total Health of the living).

tests.call: WaveSpawner.PlanWave(1)
tests.name: plan wave 1

tests.call: WaveSpawner.PlanWave(3)
tests.name: plan wave 3

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var w = new WaveSpawner(); var log = new List<string>(); w.WaveStarted += (s, n) => log.Add("start " + n); w.WaveCleared += (s, n) => log.Add("clear " + n); var sq = w.SpawnNext(); foreach (var u in sq.Alive) u.TakeDamage(999); w.SpawnNext(); return string.Join(", ", log) + " | kills " + w.Kills; }))()
tests.name: events in order

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var w = new WaveSpawner(); string before = w.Summary(); var sq = w.SpawnNext(); sq.Alive[0].TakeDamage(12); return before + " | " + w.Summary(); }))()
tests.expect: No wave yet | Wave 1: 2/2 alive, 90 HP left
tests.name: summary

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var w = new WaveSpawner(); for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) foreach (var u in w.SpawnNext().Alive) u.TakeDamage(999); var sq = w.SpawnNext(); return w.Wave + " " + sq.Count + " " + sq.Strongest; }))()
tests.name: wave 3 brings a captain

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var w = new WaveSpawner(); w.SpawnNext(); w.SpawnNext(); return "no error"; }))()
tests.name: can't skip a wave

tests.call: WaveSpawner.PlanWave(0)
tests.name: wave 0

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var w = new WaveSpawner(); var sq = w.SpawnNext(); sq.Alive[0].TakeDamage(999); return w.Summary() + " | kills " + w.Kills; }))()
tests.name: half the wave down

hints: PlanWave: a for loop from 1 to wave + 1 adding $"Grunt {i}"; then if (wave % 3 == 0) names[names.Count - 1] = "Captain";
In SpawnNext: Unit u = name == "Captain" ? new Knight(name) : new Soldier(name); u.Died += OnEnemyDied; squad.Add(u);
private void OnEnemyDied(object sender, EventArgs e) { Kills++; if (Enemies.Alive.Count == 0) WaveCleared?.Invoke(this, Wave); }

exercises.title: Prove the spawner plan
exercises.prompt:
Spawner.PlanWave (the correct rules from Part 2) is given. Write SpawnerChecks.AllPass(Func<int, List<string>> planWave): use your own checks to decide whether the function you are given follows ALL the rules:
  wave n gives n + 1 names; they are "Grunt 1", "Grunt 2"... in order; on every third wave (3, 6, 9...) the last name is "Captain" and on other waves there is no Captain; wave 0 or below throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException.
Return true only if every check passes. Never throw: if the function crashes where it should give an answer, that's a false. Archie runs it on the real PlanWave (must be true) and on broken versions (must be false).

tests.call: SpawnerChecks.AllPass(Spawner.PlanWave).ToString()
tests.name: the real plan passes

tests.call: SpawnerChecks.AllPass(n => { if (n < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(); var l = new List<string>(); for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) l.Add("Grunt " + i); if (n % 3 == 0) l[l.Count - 1] = "Captain"; return l; }).ToString()
tests.name: catches: one enemy too few

tests.call: SpawnerChecks.AllPass(n => { if (n < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(); var l = new List<string>(); for (int i = 1; i <= n + 1; i++) l.Add("Grunt " + i); if (true) l[l.Count - 1] = "Captain"; return l; }).ToString()
tests.name: catches: a captain every wave

tests.call: SpawnerChecks.AllPass(n => { if (n < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(); var l = new List<string>(); for (int i = 1; i <= n + 1; i++) l.Add("Grunt " + i); if (false) l[l.Count - 1] = "Captain"; return l; }).ToString()
tests.name: catches: no captain ever

tests.call: SpawnerChecks.AllPass(n => { if (n < 1) return new List<string>(); var l = new List<string>(); for (int i = 1; i <= n + 1; i++) l.Add("Grunt " + i); if (n % 3 == 0) l[l.Count - 1] = "Captain"; return l; }).ToString()
tests.name: catches: wave 0 doesn't throw
tests.hint_if_fail: Check that planWave(0) throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException, inside a try/catch.

tests.call: SpawnerChecks.AllPass(n => { if (n < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(); var l = new List<string>(); for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) l.Add("Grunt " + i); if (n % 3 == 0) l[l.Count - 1] = "Captain"; return l; }).ToString()
tests.name: catches: numbering starts at 0
tests.hint_if_fail: Check the actual names, not just the count.

tests.call: SpawnerChecks.AllPass(n => { if (n < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(); var l = new List<string>(); for (int i = 1; i <= n + 1; i++) l.Add("Grunt " + i); if (n == 3) l[l.Count - 1] = "Captain"; return l; }).ToString()
tests.name: catches: captain only on wave 3
tests.hint_if_fail: Check wave 6 too, not just wave 3.

tests.call: SpawnerChecks.AllPass(n => throw new InvalidOperationException()).ToString()
tests.name: a crashing plan is a fail, not a crash

hints: Write a small helper: static bool Throws(Action a) { try { a(); return false; } catch (ArgumentOutOfRangeException) { return true; } catch (Exception) { return false; } }
Wrap the whole body of AllPass in try { ... } catch (Exception) { return false; } so a crashing version counts as a fail.

quiz.q: Why does WaveSpawner subscribe to each unit's Died event instead of units calling the spawner?
choices: Units stay independent: they work the same with or without a spawner

quiz.q: Why is PlanWave a static method returning a list, separate from SpawnNext?
choices: It's a pure function: easy to test without making units or events
quiz.why: Pure logic is the easiest code to test.

quiz.q: Squad<T> where T : Unit lets you write…
choices: Squad<Archer> and Squad<Unit>, and use u.Health inside
quiz.why: The constraint allows any Unit and its members.

quiz.q: Your SpawnerChecks only check planWave(1). Which broken version slips through?
choices: One that never makes a Captain
One that returns null for wave 1
quiz.why: Wave 1 has no Captain anyway: test wave 3 and 6 too.

quiz.q: Knight is sealed. What does that stop?

cards.q: Where do the rules of damage live?
cards.a: In Unit.TakeDamage: one place, used by every kind of unit

cards.q: How does the spawner know a wave is cleared?
cards.a: It subscribes to each enemy's Died event and checks how many are alive

cards.q: Why keep logic out of the engine?
cards.a: Plain C# classes can be tested, reused and trusted
Normal cases, every edge, bad input, and they must fail on broken versions

explain: Explain how the pieces of your battle system talk to each other (interface, base class, generic squad, events), as if to a friend who is about to add a new enemy type.
